title: Cash Flow Before Complexity
excerpt: Most planning anxiety is cash-flow anxiety in costume. We start with the arithmetic you actually live.
body: Most planning anxiety is cash-flow anxiety in costume. Before anyone draws an estate diagram or opens a product shelf, we want a plain picture of how money moves through your life: what comes in, what goes out, what sits in reserves, and what is spoken for.

That sounds obvious. It is also where a surprising number of “complex” plans fall apart. A trust that looks elegant on paper is useless if the cash you need next year is trapped somewhere you can’t reach without a tax surprise. A portfolio that beats a benchmark is cold comfort if tuition, a roof, or a parent’s care arrives and the liquidity isn’t there.

So we start with your actual arithmetic — income, spending, taxes, gifts, debt service, and the reserves you want to keep for the year that does not go as planned. Once that map is honest, the fancy decisions get smaller. Estate structure, education funding, philanthropy, and concentrated positions become tools in service of a life you already understand, not projects invented to look busy.

Technology helps us stress-test the picture against bad markets, rising taxes, and the kinds of surprises families actually meet. Judgment decides which levers matter this year. We do not use cookie-cutter templates. We build a practical blueprint, and we adjust it as your life changes.

If something outside Fairview affects the picture — a house, a business stake, an old 401(k), private holdings — we fold it into the same plan. You have one financial life. You should not have six disconnected ones.

title: Preparing Heirs Without the Speech
excerpt: Wealth transitions fail quietly. The fix is rarely a thicker binder — it is smaller, honest conversations timed to the family.
body: Wealth transitions fail quietly. Intent stays vague. Heirs are unready. Advisors who should talk to each other never meet. Then a binder arrives after the fact and everyone is surprised it did not save the day.

The fix is rarely more paper. It is a series of small, honest conversations — timed to the family, not to a calendar someone invented in a conference room. Who needs context now? What can wait? What stays private, and what should be shared so the next generation does not inherit a riddle?

We help families stage that work. Sometimes it means introducing adult children to the advisor who already knows the balance sheet. Sometimes it means walking through why a trust exists before anyone has to live inside it. Sometimes it means saying clearly what you hope money will do — and what you hope it will not.

Values do not transfer by dramatic reveal. Decision-making does not either. Continuity comes from practice: enough shared language that the people you care about can make good choices without you in the room.

Your estate lawyer, tax accountant, trustee, and philanthropic advisors should not operate in isolation. We coordinate with the professionals you already trust so nothing falls through the cracks between them — including the human parts that never show up on a spreadsheet.
The goal is not a perfect speech. It is a family that knows where things stand, and a plan that still works when life refuses to follow the outline.

title: Taxes Are a Cost. Treat Them Like One.
excerpt: We do not chase every deduction. We look at your income, assets, and goals — then use the tax code where it actually helps the plan.
body: Taxes are a cost of owning capital, earning income, and transferring wealth. They are not a personality trait, and they are not a reason to buy something you would otherwise never own. At Fairview we look at your income, assets, and goals first — then ask which tax tools help the plan you are actually living.

That usually starts with the accounts that already sit in front of you. Workplace plans, IRAs, and similar vehicles can lower taxable income today, grow with deferred tax, or (in Roth form) trade a deduction now for tax-free withdrawals later. Matching contributions, when offered, are simply free money — take them before you look for cleverer ideas. Contribution limits change; we work from the current rules with your tax professional, not from last year’s brochure.

Roth conversions are a different question. High earners often cannot contribute directly to a Roth IRA, but converting traditional balances can still make sense in a lower-income year, between careers, or in the window before required distributions and Social Security raise the bracket. The trade is simple arithmetic: pay tax now at a known rate, or later at an unknown one. We run that math with your CPA — not as a slogan.

Education savings, health savings accounts, and charitable giving sit in the same category: useful when they match a real intent. A 529 helps if school costs are coming. An HSA helps if you have the right health plan and medical expenses to fund. Giving appreciated stock to a charity or donor-advised fund can be cleaner than selling first and writing a check — if you were going to give anyway.

Inside the portfolio, tax awareness is quieter work. Harvesting losses to offset gains. Preferring municipal bonds when after-tax yield beats the taxable alternative. Avoiding unnecessary turnover. Coordinating sales across accounts so one year’s “win” does not become next April’s surprise. Every trade we make accounts for taxes. That is not a side service; it is how the portfolio is run.

What we do not do is rearrange your life around a tip sheet. Product shelves and year-end “strategies” that ignore cash flow, risk, and family goals are how people buy complexity. The useful tax plan is the one that still makes sense when the code changes — because the life underneath it was the point all along.

title: Choosing a Trustee Is the Hard Part
excerpt: A trust is only as good as the person or institution asked to run it. Pick for judgment, not for flattery.
body: A trust can be a sensible way to hold and pass assets — steadier than an outright will gift when you care about how money is managed, protected, and distributed over time. It can also fail in ordinary ways: the wrong person in charge, unclear instructions, or a structure nobody revisits after the signing ceremony.

In a trust, beneficiaries do not simply receive title the way they might under a will. You hand management authority to a trustee — a person, a corporate fiduciary, or both — to invest, protect, and distribute according to the document. That is a real job. It involves judgment, paperwork, family diplomacy, and the occasional hard no.

So start with competence. Individual trustees need enough financial sense to know when they are out of their depth, and the humility to hire help. Corporate trustees bring process and continuity, and they charge for it. Match the skill to the purpose: investment-heavy trusts want investment literacy; legally delicate ones want people who respect counsel; tax-sensitive ones need someone who will not improvise with the IRS.

Then look at character without romance. How does this person run their own affairs? Can they be fair when they are also a beneficiary? Will they favor one branch of the family? Age matters too — a peer may not outlast you, and a spouse who remarries may face pressures you never intended. Agreeing with why the trust exists is not optional. If they think the whole idea is wrong, do not put them in charge of it.

Co-trustees can blend family knowledge with institutional muscle. They can also create deadlock, delay, and higher administration. Use them when the mix of skills is worth the friction — not as a peace offering that papers over a conflict you already see coming.

Finally, leave room to revisit. Lives change. Laws change. A trust built for tuition may outlive that need. A trustee who was right at forty may be wrong at seventy. We work alongside your estate attorney — coordinating with accountants and other advisors — so the document and the people named in it still match the family you have, not the family you had when the binder was new.

title: Legacy Is a Practice, Not a Slogan
excerpt: Assets transfer on paper. Judgment transfers only if you teach it — on purpose, while there is still time.
body: People say they want generational wealth. What they usually mean is something more specific: children who can stand on their own, a cause that outlasts them, a business that does not implode in the handoff, or a family that still speaks to each other after the estate closes.

Start there — with purpose — before you start with vehicles. Do you care about schools, land, a company, philanthropy, or simply enough capital that the next generation is not improvising under pressure? “Legacy” that means everything means nothing. Two or three clear aims beat a binder full of options.

Then say it out loud. Families lose wealth for many reasons; silence is one of the reliable ones. Heirs who never heard the plan cannot defend it. Heirs who only hear about money in a crisis often treat money as the crisis. Share enough, early enough, that values are practiced — trips that teach what you care about, introductions to the business, real conversations about giving — not a single dramatic reveal after the fact.

Prudence still matters. A plan that ignores taxes, liquidity, and concentration risk is a hope costume. Annual gifting, trusts, and charitable gifts of appreciated assets can help when they serve the purpose you already named. We run those tools with your attorneys and accountants; we do not sell them as personality.

Investing is part of the same story. We focus on long-term ownership of quality businesses researched in-house — the slow work of knowing what we own — so capital has a chance to compound across the decades a real legacy needs. Planning without a portfolio thesis is half a plan. A portfolio without a family thesis is just a statement.

We keep the whole picture together: the assets we manage and the ones we do not, the people who advise you, and the generations who will eventually sit where you sit now. Continuity is the product. Marketing copy about “the Fairview difference” is not.

title: Helping Adult Children Without Breaking the Plan
excerpt: Most parents help somehow. The question is whether the help builds independence — and whether your own retirement still works afterward.
body: Most parents help adult children somehow — rent, tuition, loan payments, a first down payment, a stretch on the family payroll. In places like the Bay Area, where housing and education costs have outrun young wages for years, that impulse is easy to understand. Understanding it does not make every check wise.

Start with your own arithmetic. You are allowed to put your retirement, reserves, and health first. A gift that leaves you exposed to a bad market, a long care need, or a forced sale of assets is not generosity; it is a transfer of risk onto the people you were trying to protect. Before you write the number, stress-test a few hard years. If the plan only works in the good scenario, it is not a plan.

Then ask what the help is building. Scaffolding toward self-sufficiency — finishing school, bridging an internship, seeding a home purchase with a clear ceiling — is different from an open tab that replaces a career or postpones hard choices. One-time capital that launches something is usually cleaner than indefinite subsidy. If resentment is already in the room, money will not remove it.

Family dynamics matter as much as the spreadsheet. Helping one child may raise fairness questions with siblings. Being asked may feel fine — or it may feel like a second job you never applied for. Say the terms out loud. Amount, purpose, end date. If it is a loan, write it down like a loan. Ambiguity is how ordinary families invent lawsuits.

We help clients size support against the rest of the picture: cash flow, taxes, estate intent, and the assets outside the accounts we manage. Sometimes the right answer is yes, with boundaries. Sometimes it is a smaller number. Sometimes it is help of a different kind — introductions, budgeting, or a clear no delivered early enough to still be kind.

Parents want the best for their kids. The best version usually includes adult children who can stand without leaning forever — and parents who can still fund their own lives when the markets and the medicine bills arrive on schedule.

title: Rotation, Then Shock
excerpt: Ending 2025, US equity markets had enjoyed three consecutive strong years and were poised for continued upside. The economy showed resilience, absorbing tariffs and a government shutdown, while inflation remained…
body: Ending 2025, US equity markets had enjoyed three consecutive strong years and were poised for continued upside. The economy showed resilience, absorbing tariffs and a government shutdown, while inflation remained relatively muted and on a downtrend. Corporate earnings growth accelerated, fueling expectations for mid-teens growth in the first quarter. The Fed signaled additional rate cuts, bolstering the case for ongoing market strength.

Equity markets experienced a notable rotation in the first quarter as the market navigated AI-driven concerns and private credit issues before the Iran conflict delivered an unforeseen disruption in late February. A rotation out of the tech sector into defensive stocks left the markets flat going into the war.

The Iran conflict has negatively impacted equity and bond markets due to spiking oil prices and fears of stagflationary impacts on the global economy. For the first quarter the S&P 500 index total return was down 4.4%, the NASDAQ declined 7.0% and the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index generated a slightly negative return. As we reach mid-April, the equity markets have turned positive for the year.

Entering the second quarter, several issues – AI disruption and a possible bubble, private credit contagion, unsettled tariff policy and global economic stress resulting from the oil shock – are presenting challenges to the bull market’s staying power. Equity market valuations remain high at 19.7x forward earnings estimates relative to the 30-year average of 17.2x.
From a macro perspective, divergent scenarios – a strong economy and moderating inflation vs. stagflation (recession and high inflation) – have reasonably high probabilities.
pullQuote: From a macro perspective, divergent scenarios – a strong economy and moderating inflation vs. stagflation (recession and high inflation) – have reasonably high probabilities.

title: A Third Year of Gains
excerpt: Equity markets enjoyed a third consecutive year of gains, with the S&P 500 index advancing 17.9%. After the tariff shock in early April amid concerns of stagflationary impacts, the market rallied from April 8th lows and…
body: Equity markets enjoyed a third consecutive year of gains, with the S&P 500 index advancing 17.9%. After the tariff shock in early April amid concerns of stagflationary impacts, the market rallied from April 8th lows and appreciated throughout the year. Gains were fueled by resilient GDP growth, strong consumer spending, robust corporate earnings, relatively muted inflation and interest rate cuts.

Heading into the sustained economic resilience of 2026, accelerated earnings growth with the possibility of both fiscal and monetary stimulus could lead to further market appreciation. Issues that could derail markets or cause increased volatility are historically high valuations, the soft labor market, fiscal excess (which at some point will pressure long-term interest rates and further pressure the dollar) and geopolitical tensions.

Recent headlines about an AI bubble are constructive and volatility in the space between AI winners and losers is encouraging, leading us to believe any AI bubble may deflate rather than pop. There is no question that AI is transformative and not going away, but the AI narrative versus reality has led to some extreme and unsustainable near-term stock price activity. We see AI itself as a commoditizing tool facilitated by mass digitization, with the greatest benefits accruing to those companies throughout the economy that implement it into work flows to drive revenue and profit growth. The market is beginning to look beyond the AI narrative to reality as it sorts out long-term winners and losers in the space.

The current administration has been implementing aggressive policies while pursuing their objectives of accelerating economic growth and vibrancy of the domestic manufacturing base. Their playbook to “run the economy hot” would lead to an accelerating cyclical recovery along with the potential for higher inflation.

Amid the foregoing opportunities and risks, our investment strategy is to participate in market upside while positioning to navigate the uncertainties. To mitigate inflation and currency risks our portfolio includes many investments with pricing power/flexibility and hard assets, as well as selective international exposure. Fixed income remains an asset to mitigate volatility.
pullQuote: Recent headlines about an AI bubble are constructive and volatility in the space between AI winners and losers is encouraging, leading us to believe any AI bubble may deflate rather than pop.

title: Resilience, Then the First Cut
excerpt: We entered the third quarter amidst tariff uncertainties and concerns for a slowing economy. The economy has remained resilient, with quarterly GDP growth exceeding 3%. Consumer spending and income growth have outpaced…
body: We entered the third quarter amidst tariff uncertainties and concerns for a slowing economy. The economy has remained resilient, with quarterly GDP growth exceeding 3%. Consumer spending and income growth have outpaced inflation thus far. Corporate earnings continue to meet or even beat expectations, and we anticipate this trend to continue as third quarter earnings reports start coming in. Inflation has edged higher but remains in check, albeit nearly 1% higher than the Fed’s 2% inflation target.

Further boosting equities, on September 17 the Fed initiated a new rate cutting cycle with a 25-basis point cut to the Fed Funds rate and clear signals that two more cuts are likely this year. New job growth has been weak while the unemployment rate remains stable.

Against this backdrop equity market returns have been robust, with the S&P 500 advancing 8.1% and 14.8% for the third quarter and year to date respectively. Corporate operating fundamentals are strong heading into the fourth quarter, while valuations remain at historically high levels. These valuations are at odds with ongoing issues such as tariff and trade policies, directives impacting Fed independence, the government shutdown, geopolitical tensions and the Federal Deficit.

The advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is driving equity markets and impacting the economy in new, and thus far, positive ways. Massive capital spending on AI infrastructure has been embraced by financial markets, however the timing, feasibility and expected return on this multi trillion-dollar investment has recently been called into question. Parallels to the late nineties dotcom boom – and eventual bust – have been surfacing.

We are evaluating other grounded AI beneficiaries based on proven use cases to drive growth and margins. We are closely monitoring implementation of AI in areas such as software and digital advertising to identify favorable and unfavorable impacts. We will avoid excessive valuations and/or speculative business models that lack clarity. Inevitable surprises and exogenous factors will occur, and we are mindful of the risks.

Befitting solid economic and stock market fundamentals, equities closed the third quarter near all-time highs. Economic growth in the coming year will likely be driven by tax, trade and policy initiatives, but a fractured Congress could limit meaningful legislation. We believe rising inflation remains a major risk to financial asset valuations.
pullQuote: We believe rising inflation remains a major risk to financial asset valuations.

title: From Liberation Day to New Highs
excerpt: A volatile and historic quarter closed at all-time highs for the S&P 500 and NASDAQ Composite, which advanced 10.9% and 18.0% respectively. The quarter began with “Liberation Day” tariffs which sent markets tumbling.…
body: A volatile and historic quarter closed at all-time highs for the S&P 500 and NASDAQ Composite, which advanced 10.9% and 18.0% respectively. The quarter began with “Liberation Day” tariffs which sent markets tumbling. After bottoming on April 8 (at which point the S&P 500 and NASDAQ were down 15.0% and 20.8% for the year), equity markets moved steadily higher supported by tariff easing, solid first quarter earnings, bottoming consumer sentiment and resilient macroeconomic reads for inflation and the economy. The market plunge and rapid recovery reminds us how quickly equity markets can shift.

Much of the second quarter, appreciation was fueled by digitization and Artificial Intelligence (AI) themes. Among the “Magnificent 7”, Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA advanced 35.6% on average. Amazon, Google, Apple and Tesla were up 11.0% due to perception that they are less well positioned for AI and/or have greater exposure to trade policy.

Entering the third quarter, equity and bond markets are navigating concerns over the economic and inflationary impacts of tariffs, geopolitical disruptions and U.S. fiscal policy. Leading economists and the Federal Reserve bank are signaling stagflationary conditions (slowing economic growth paired with rising inflation), while equity markets are anticipating continued growth with modest pressure on inflation.

Expected earnings growth for 2025 began the year at 14.3% and has been revised down to 9.4% currently, with 13.7% growth expected for 2026. Amidst a high level of uncertainty, the equity markets sit at historically high valuations. The S&P 500 index trades at a forward price to earnings multiple of 22x as compared to the past ten-year historical average of 18.7x.

A significant decline in equities is possible. However, if the economy holds up and inflation does not materialize, corporate earnings will accelerate and would likely be boosted by Fed rate cuts. This could bring cautious capital into the market and propel equities higher from here. In sum, we continue to expect a high level of volatility of share prices during the second half of 2025.
pullQuote: The market plunge and rapid recovery reminds us how quickly equity markets can shift.

title: The Streak Breaks
excerpt: After six consecutive quarterly gains, the S&P 500 index declined 4.3% and the NASDAQ index dropped 10.3% in this year’s first quarter. The year started with gains in January and February, navigating a rotation out of…
body: After six consecutive quarterly gains, the S&P 500 index declined 4.3% and the NASDAQ index dropped 10.3% in this year’s first quarter. The year started with gains in January and February, navigating a rotation out of the Tech sector and into lagging sectors, most notably consumer staples, healthcare and energy. March saw a broad sell-off as the S&P 500 index declined 5.6%, including an 8.5% drop from the mid-February market peak. April thus far has seen further selling amidst increasing levels of volatility.

Far more damaging to equity markets than the tech rotation and downdraft has been the new administration’s aggressive and unpredictable tariff policies. We expect higher tariffs will create inflationary and economic headwinds. The uncertainty and ever-changing headlines impair economic activity, spending decisions and erode consumer confidence and sentiment.

Although the economy has been resilient and growing, recent macro-economic data points demonstrate increased concerns. Sentiment indexes have fallen sharply, with consumer confidence hitting a 12-year low in the quarter. The Fed’s projection of 2025 gross domestic product (GDP) growth declined from 2.1% at the beginning of the year to 1.7% last month.

The probability of stagflation (a recession combined with inflation, last seen in the decade of the 1970s) will increase with the implementation of tariffs. A global trade war would further impede the Fed’s best efforts to engineer a soft landing (moderating GDP growth and low inflation) that seemed possible at the start of the new administration.

With the government debt now at $36 trillion and growing, the current administration is focusing on reducing interest rates. A tariff induced recession might succeed in achieving further rate declines and stability but if high inflation accompanies the recession, a continued downtrend and the malaise of a bear market could be in store.

Fairview’s investment strategy is to position for multiple scenarios by holding best-in-class stocks at reasonable valuations across the sector spectrum. We are invested in several companies addressing market niches that are less exposed to the broader economic cycle. In these dynamic and challenging times, we are monitoring developments closely.
pullQuote: Far more damaging to equity markets than the tech rotation and downdraft has been the new administration’s aggressive and unpredictable tariff policies.

title: A 25% Year, Narrowly Won
excerpt: Despite a soft December, the U.S. equity markets closed the fourth quarter with a solid 2.4% gain. The benchmark S&P 500 generated a 25% return for the year. Slightly more than 1/5th of this return came from the…
body: Despite a soft December, the U.S. equity markets closed the fourth quarter with a solid 2.4% gain. The benchmark S&P 500 generated a 25% return for the year. Slightly more than 1/5th of this return came from the semi-conductor design firm NVIDIA, which rode the artificial intelligence boom to grow into the second largest company in the index, trailing only Apple.

Like the comparably high equity returns seen in calendar 2023, the largest contributors to the S&P 500 index returns were the mega-cap technology stocks branded as “the Magnificent Seven”: Apple, NVIDIA, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, META and Tesla. These stocks grew faster than their underlying operating fundamentals as many of these companies are seen as major beneficiaries of the expected growth of artificial intelligence.

The past two years continued the strong trend of equities outperforming fixed income by a considerable and nearly unprecedented degree. These disproportionate gains leave equities trading at unusually high multiples of revenues, earnings and cash flow. By some measures the stock market is trading at such historically high valuations that these levels are surpassed by only the peak of the dotcom bubble in the late nineties.

We expect to see a high degree of volatility in financial asset pricing in the year ahead. Data relating to economic growth, job growth and inflation remains mixed; most recently data on both economic and job growth surprised to the upside while the Producer and Consumer Pricing Indexes came in below expectations. Bond yields have risen substantially since the Federal Reserve commenced rate cuts this past September, leaving investors questioning the need for further rate cuts.

Volatility is also likely given the potential policy changes floated by the incoming administration. Bond investors are anxious regarding fiscal, trade, and immigration policies articulated thus far. Such worries are exacerbated by the prospects of much higher public borrowings and persistent inflation owing to deficit-financed domestic demand, possible tariffs and rising import prices. Geopolitical concerns and the costs of dealing with increasingly volatile weather could also weigh heavily on global financial markets.

Given these concerns, we expect to mitigate risk by maintaining investments in high-quality companies with solid balance sheets and stable cash flows. In balanced portfolios we will hold fixed income securities in short and intermediate maturities.
pullQuote: By some measures the stock market is trading at such historically high valuations that these levels are surpassed by only the peak of the dotcom bubble in the late nineties.

title: Quality Over Narrative
excerpt: Markets love a clean story. We buy the business underneath the ticker — or we wait.
body: Markets love a clean story. A ticker is just a string of letters. We buy what is underneath it.

Narratives move prices faster than balance sheets do. Artificial intelligence, policy shifts, fashion, fear — each can open a door worth walking through. None of them is a substitute for understanding cash generation, reinvestment needs, competitive position, and the price you are asked to pay for that stream of outcomes.

Most wealth managers are middlemen. They collect a fee to hand capital to someone else’s process or a model that never met the management team. We built an in-house research team to do the slower work: study the business, build a view of how it competes years out, and wait until the arithmetic makes sense. We often track a company for years before we own a share.

When a story runs ahead of the business, we wait for the business to catch up — or we pass. Showing our work means saying what we own, why we own it, and what would make us change our minds. That is not theater. It is how you avoid confusing a popular plot with a durable franchise.
It is a much slower way to operate than chasing whatever is fashionable on Wall Street. It is also the only way we know how to be sure of what we own.

title: Risk Is Not Volatility
excerpt: Price swings are uncomfortable. Permanent loss of capital is the risk that funds — or fails — a life.
body: Volatility is the language of screens. Risk is the language of families who need capital to fund a life — tuition, a business transition, a long retirement, a gift that still means something after inflation.

A temporary decline in a good business is not the same thing as owning a fragile one that cannot survive a hard year. The first is uncomfortable. The second is how permanent loss sneaks in while everyone is watching the wrong number.

We do not predict the future. We prepare for several of them. That means position sizing, cash reserves, tax-aware trading, and an allocation built around your plan — not a model portfolio that ignores the year you actually need money. Stock selection matters. So does not being forced to sell the right company at the wrong time.

Computers draw straight lines into the future. Real markets do not. We use software to stress-test plans against bad markets and rising taxes, not to pretend certainty. The research note is only half the job. The other half is making sure a rough quarter does not become a permanent mistake.
Crises come and go. Discipline is staying invested in businesses we understand, at prices we can defend, inside a plan that still works when the tape looks ugly.

title: The Reality of Banking
excerpt: SVB looked fine until it wasn’t. Banking still runs on confidence — and confidence is not a free lunch.
body: In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank went from “well capitalized, no asset-quality problems” to FDIC receivership in a matter of days. A smaller crypto lender had failed just before and been dismissed as a crypto story. SVB was not. Signature Bank followed over the weekend. By Monday, investors were asking the only question that matters in a panic: who is next?

The authorities moved fast — broader deposit backstops, easier emergency borrowing, pressure for rescues abroad. Deposit money shifted from smaller banks toward larger ones. Contagion, for the moment, was contained. That was not luck alone. It was a reminder that modern banking still depends on someone catching the plate before it hits the floor.

SVB was also an unusual bank. Its customers were a tight circle of venture firms and startups. Uninsured deposits made up the overwhelming share of funding. Pandemic-era inflows had nowhere useful to lend, so management parked cash in long-duration Treasuries. When rates rose, the paper losses were larger than at banks whose assets float with rates. When those interconnected depositors smelled trouble, they did the rational thing all at once: they asked for their money back.

Management deserved blame too. Risk systems had been flagged for years. Warnings sat unanswered. For a stretch, there was no chief risk officer. You can call SVB a special case — concentrated funding, weak controls, the sharpest rate rise in a generation — and you would not be wrong. Special cases are still how systems learn what they forgot.

After a scare, bankers relearn interest-rate risk the way they relearned asset quality after 2008. Emergency facilities, lower uninsured-deposit concentrations at most peers, and talk of tighter rules for mid-sized banks all lower the odds of an identical rerun. They do not rewrite the basic math: banks borrow short, lend long, and keep only a fraction on hand. If everyone wants cash at 9 a.m. on a Tuesday, even a strong bank is in trouble by noon. Confidence is the product. It has always been.

For investors and depositors, the lesson is dull and durable. Watch diversification of assets and liabilities. Ask how rate risk is controlled. Respect insurance limits even when rules got stretched once and will likely get stretched again. We study banks the way we study any business — balance sheet, incentives, and what breaks when the story turns. Fashionable calm after a rescue is not the same thing as risk having gone to zero.

title: When Good News Is Bad News
excerpt: Strong jobs numbers can send stocks down. Headline data lies by omission. Bring a shovel.
body: On a Friday in early 2023, the jobs report landed hot: hundreds of thousands more payrolls than expected. Equities fell. Bond yields jumped. An observer could be forgiven for wondering what, exactly, counted as good news anymore.

Ordinarily, more jobs mean more spending, more growth, and better earnings — and stocks like that story. Sometimes the tape flips the logic. When inflation is already a problem, strong data can mean the Fed stays higher for longer, recession risk rises, and “good” becomes “bad” before lunch. Knowing which regime you are in matters more than memorizing the headline.

The data itself is slippery. Seasonal adjustments can turn a raw decline in January hiring into a soaring seasonally adjusted print. First releases are estimates; later benchmarks revise them. Catch-up hiring in industries still climbing out of a shock can look like boom-time strength until the catch-up ends. First impressions of economic releases mislead often enough that treating them as gospel is a hobby, not a process.

Indicators also quarrel. A tight unemployment rate can sit beside cooling wage growth. Measures of labor-market “slack” that only count the officially unemployed miss people returning to the workforce. Participation can rise quietly in the background and change the whole story about wage pressure. Wall Street likes tidy chains of cause and effect. The economy is under no obligation to provide them.

We do not pretend to predict every print. We prepare for several futures: watch inflation and policy, read past the seasonally adjusted theater, and ask what a number implies for cash flows and valuations — not what it implies for tomorrow’s open. Macro work is an inexact science. Most forecasts are wrong. Probabilities and second looks are the job.
Interpretation of economic data should come with caution and a large shovel. Dig once. Then decide whether anything in the portfolio should actually change.
